blocks.text: Sprinkled with the winter snows, the gentle hen spread her sleep-bringing wings over her chicks, until the cold of the sky killed her. Truly she held out as a fighter against the clouds of heaven. O mothers, Procne and Medea, blush in the underworld, as you learn the works of hens. And the excellent writer Plutarch, in the book On Affection for Offspring, sets the matter before our eyes thus: Τὰς δὲ ἀλεκτορίδας ἐν τοῖς ὄμμασι καθ᾽ ἡμέραν ἔχομεν, ὃν τρόπον τὰ νεοττία περιέπουσι, τοῖς μὲν ἐνδῦναι χαλῶσαι τὰς πτέρυγας, τὰ δὲ ἐπιβαίνοντα τῶν νώτων, καὶ προσέρχονται πανταχόθεν ἀναδεχόμεναι, μετὰ τοῦ γεγηθὸς, ἢ καὶ προσφιλὲς ἐπιφθέγγεσθαι. κυνέας δὲ, καὶ δρακοντίας [Tas de alektoridas en tois ommasi kath᾽ hēmeran echomen, hon tropon ta neottia periepousi, tois men endynai chalōsai tas pterygas, ta de epibainonta tōn nōtōn, kai proserchontai pantachothen anadechomenai, meta tou gegēthos, ē kai prosphiles epiphthengesthai. kyneas de, kai drakontias] (read κύνας δὲ, καὶ δράκοντας [kynas de, kai drakontas], or δρακόντια [drakontia]) ἂν περὶ αὐτῶν φοβηθῶσι φεύγουσιν· ἂν δὲ περὶ τῶν τέκνων, ἀμύνονται, καὶ διαμάχονται παρὰ δύναμιν [an peri autōn phobēthōsi pheugousin; an de peri tōn teknōn, amynontai, kai diamachontai para dynamin]. And hens, which are before our eyes every day: with what care they protect their chicks, letting down their wings for some to creep under, while others climb onto their backs! And they come up from every side to receive them, so as to testify their joy and love with their voice. Dogs and serpents, if they fear for themselves, flee; but if they fear for their young, they drive off the attacker and fight beyond their strength. Augustine observes this very thing in these words in the Gospel Questions, book 1, question 36: What you will find with greater difficulty in other animals, protecting her young with her wings she [II, 697] fights against the kite. But he also often asserts that it is peculiar to the hen that she is so affected by the weakness of her chicks that she herself becomes weak and sick. Thus on Psalm 58: He (Christ) was made weak even unto death, and took on the flesh of weakness, in order to gather the chicks of Jerusalem under his wings, as the hen becomes weak with her little ones. And a little later: Surely I speak of a well-known thing, which is before our eyes every day. How her voice grows hoarse! How her whole body becomes bristly, her wings droop, her feathers loosen! And on Psalm XC.: Many birds here breed before our eyes and warm their chicks; no bird becomes weak with her chicks as the hen does. Let your charity consider swallows, sparrows and storks. We see them outside their nests, and we do not know whether they have young. But the hen we recognize by the weakness of her voice and the loosening of her feathers: she is wholly changed by affection for her chicks; because they are weak, she makes herself weak. And in On the Words of the Lord, Sermon 29: That hen is the wisdom of the Lord. But it took on flesh in order to be suited to the chicks. See the hen, bristling in her feathers, wings lowered, voice broken, shaken, weary and languid, suiting herself to her chicks. And in the Questions cited above: This kind of animal has great affection for its young, so that, affected by their weakness, it too becomes weak. Hence in Euripides, in the Madness of Heracles, Megara, greatly anxious about the children she had borne to Hercules, repeatedly says that she keeps them under her wings, like a hen brooding her chicks. The words are:

Οἵ θ᾽ Ἡράκλειοι παῖδες, οὓς ὑποπτέρους Σώζω νεοσσοὺς, ὄρνις ὡς ὑφειμένη· [Hoi th᾽ Hērakleioi paides, hous hypopterous Sōzō neossous, ornis hōs hypheimenē] And the sons of Hercules, whom under my wings I keep, as a hen is wont to brood her chicks.

I adduce these things here because they are very similar to the words of Christ, in which he compares his φιλανθρωπίαν [philanthrōpian] with the φιλοστοργίᾳ [philostorgia] of the hen, which with the greatest eagerness draws her chicks to herself, in order to keep them safe and sound under her wings from the threatening kite or hawk.
